Thanks for the time this morning, Jordan — quick recap and the next steps we discussed. Great to meet Sanjay as well (on the procurement thread).

Recap (short):
- Workload: customer-facing summarization + retrieval-augmented responses (avg input+output ~150 tokens/request).
- Expected steady-state: ~40 QPS during peak; concurrency spiky up to 120 QPS for short bursts.
- Latency SLO: p95 <= 200ms (goal: 150ms).
- Key concerns you raised: predictable unit cost (per-1M tokens), model fallbacks, and ability to enforce KMS for keys.

High-level positioning vs hyperscalers (preview of numbers — details in the attached spreadsheet):
- Redwood (hosted, optimized runtime): focuses on batching + prefix/KV caching + quantization-friendly profiles that reduce effective generation tokens.
- Hyperscalers (managed endpoints): generally higher per-token list price; fewer inference optimizations by default unless you self-manage.

Proposed immediate tests (what we agreed):
1) 3-day comparative run: Redwood hosted endpoint vs [customer-chosen hyperscaler endpoint]. We'll capture p50/p95 latencies, end-to-end cost, and 1M-token unit economics under your workload profile.
2) Cache hit validation: run a week of representative traffic to estimate realistic KV/prefix cache hit rate (we typically see 20–40% on retrieval-heavy apps).
3) Failure/fallback test: simulate overloaded zone to verify automatic routing to fallback model variants.

Next steps / asks:
- Jordan: confirm target model family (e.g., llama-2-70b-like or 13b) and provide a short sample corpus for caching tests (ideally ~5k queries).
- Sanjay: I’ve attached a short mutual-action-plan and an initial TCO workbook for procurement review. Could you share procurement timeline?
- Marcus: once Jordan confirms model and corpus, can you provision the 3-day test config and drop the run link here?

Attachments: redwood-tco-vs-hyperscalers.xlsx (cost breakout), mutual-action-plan.pdf

Thanks — I’ll follow up with a more detailed per-1M token breakdown in the next email.

Great questions — below is the concise per-1M token breakdown and the assumptions we used (also captured in the attached spreadsheet). I’ll flag the variable line-items so procurement can see levers we control.

Assumptions (for all numbers below): average request = 150 tokens total (30 input, 120 output); batching at avg batch size 8 for Redwood during peak; KV/prefix cache hit rate baseline 30% (we’ll validate). Dedicated vs hosted line items differ (see notes).

Redwood (hosted, optimized runtime) — effective unit economics per 1,000,000 tokens:
- Raw tokens processed: 1,000,000
- Compute (GPU time amortized, incl batching & optimized kernels): $6.50
- Model serving license & infra: $2.75
- Networking & storage (KV lookups, small): $0.60
- Operational overhead & SLA premium: $1.15
- Effective discounts from caching (30% hit) & batching: net reduction: -$0.90
= Total: $10.10 per 1M tokens

Hyperscaler (managed endpoint — single-zone, list prices, no specialized KV caching):
- Raw tokens processed: 1,000,000
- Compute & managed infra: $18.00
- Networking & storage: $1.20
- Operational overhead / higher list price margin: $2.50
= Total: $21.70 per 1M tokens

Notes / levers:
- Cache hit delta: each +10ppt cache hit reduces Redwood effective cost by roughly $0.30–$0.45 per 1M tokens depending on interaction pattern (prefix vs full generation avoidance).
- Batching: better batching improves GPU utilization; moving from batch=4 -> batch=12 can reduce compute unit cost by ~20% in our workload tests.
- Quantization profiles: using int8/int4 profiles on dedicated pools can reduce compute costs further (we can show a Dedicated TCO sheet if you want committed capacity math).
- Latency trade-offs: lower cost configurations (larger batching, heavier quant) may increase tail latency; we’ll include p95 measurements in the test.

Proposed next test concretely:
- 72-hour head-to-head using the same model family & sample corpus you provide. Measure: total tokens, p50/p95 latency, throughput, cache hit rates, and end-to-end cost.
- Deliverable: a side-by-side TCO with sensitivity to cache hit rate and batching.

I’ve attached the workbook redwood-tco-vs-hyperscalers.xlsx with the full line-item math and a scenario tab (delta by cache hit % and batch size). Marcus — can you provision the test config (hosted endpoint + metrics dashboard) after Jordan confirms the sample corpus?

Thanks — happy to hop on a short call to walk procurement through the workbook.

—
Aditya Rao
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
